title: Crumbs under the table (Mark 7:24–30)
hookLine: a Syrophoenician mother talks back to Jesus and wins
carry: even the dogs eat the crumbs

lines: A HOUSE, AND NO ONE TO KNOW.
cards: Jesus slips into a house and wants nobody to know he's there. He has gone north, over the border, to the borders of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the coast. It doesn't work: Mark says he could not be hid.
A woman finds him. She isn't Jewish, and she has no claim on him at all. But her young daughter has an unclean spirit, Mark says, and the mother falls at his feet and begs.
What follows is an uncomfortable conversation, and readers still argue over it.

teach.b: Mark tells us exactly who she is: "The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation." Greek-speaking, from the Phoenician coast of Syria. An outsider, in every way.

teach.h: THE CHILDREN'S BREAD, AND THE DOGS.
teach.b: And Jesus's answer, in the old King James Bible, is hard to hear: "Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs." The children are Israel.
The dogs are everyone else. Mark's Greek uses a small form of the word for dog, the kind kept in the house, but it still stings. She doesn't walk away, and she doesn't argue that she isn't one.

teach.h: YET THE DOGS EAT THE CRUMBS.
teach.b: She picks up his picture and turns it: "Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs." Fine. Then I'll take the crumbs.

Anyone who's watched kids eat knows the dog under the table eats well. And Jesus says: "For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter." She goes home and finds the child lying in bed, well.
Christians read this conversation in several ways. Some say Jesus was testing her faith, and she passed. Some say he was voicing what people around him thought, so that her answer would overturn it.
Others say plainly that she changed his mind, and that Mark lets us see it. Either way, her daughter is healed for this saying. And notice the word first.
Children first, not children only. Right after this, Jesus heads into more Gentile country. The crumbs are about to become a feast.

how: Some Christians look to the Syrophoenician woman as a model of bold, persistent prayer for others, and some churches read her story when speaking about welcome for outsiders.

o: a Jewish woman from a village by Galilee's lake
a Greek-speaking woman from the coast of Syria
a Roman official's wife living in Jerusalem

p: not meet to cast to the dogs

she was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by nation, an outsider.
Jesus says the children must be filled first

games.q: you're the mother. you've begged for your daughter, and he says the children's bread isn't for the dogs. what do you do?
o: take his picture and turn it: then give me the crumbs.
argue that you're not a dog.
games.why: yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs. for that answer, her daughter is healed.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love who needs something they can't ask for themselves: a child who needs help at school, a parent navigating doctors, a friend facing a system that keeps saying no.

Picture yourself, like this mother, refusing to take the first no as the last word, respectful, clever, stubborn, and ask what you would say. If you pray, you can bring their need to God as boldly as she did.

wordCard.voice: Syrophenician, the outsider mother, Greek-speaking from the Phoenician coast, whose sharp reply about crumbs won healing for her daughter.

orig.note: Greek: a small form of the word for dog, a house dog. still a sting.
